pitfalls: Treating a single, permanent 'kill -9' as full crash coverage — it only ever exercises crash-stop behavior; a system's WAL replay, snapshot recovery, and rejoin-after-restart logic is untested until the fault model actually reboots nodes mid-run (crash-recovery).

Injecting a stronger failure class than the system claims to tolerate (arbitrary corruption or forged messages into a merely crash-fault-tolerant system) and reporting the resulting break as a bug — Cristian's hierarchy says this was never in scope; it reconfirms a known limitation instead of finding a new one.

Modeling only network, disk, and clock faults and skipping DNS, configuration, and dependency faults — some of the highest-blast-radius real production outages (the October 2025 AWS DynamoDB DNS outage among them) are exactly this category, and a fault model that never touches it has a large, unexamined blind spot.

Assuming fsync()/write success implies durability in the strong sense most engineers expect — the actual kernel contract can be narrower (a failed writeback's pages simply dropped, not retried), so 'it returned success' and 'it's on disk' are not the same claim without verifying which contract the platform actually offers.

Injecting every fault at maximum severity, independently and simultaneously, and calling the result 'adversarial' — real failures correlate (shared power, shared network gear, one bad deploy hitting every replica together); a fault model that never samples correlated, multi-node faults under-explores the scenarios that cause the worst real incidents.

Collapsing every storage problem into one 'disk unavailable' fault — a full disk, a torn write, silent corruption of already-durable bytes, and file-system-specific reordering of metadata updates are different bugs waiting for different code paths, and a fault model that only ever removes the disk entirely leaves most of that surface untested.

claims.text: The unit of debugging value a DST run produces on failure is not a stack trace but a bundle: the seed, the exact configuration/topology drawn from it, the workload definition, the fault schedule, the full event trace, any logs, and the assertion/invariant history up to the point of failure. Persisting only a symptom (a log line, a crash message) throws away everything that made the run reproducible in the first place; persisting the bundle is what turns "a bug happened once" into "a bug I can make happen again, right now, on my laptop."

TigerBeetle's VOPR ties this bundle to two numbers, not one: the random seed and the exact Git commit the simulation ran against. When a run fails, the developer gets both back and a precise trace of how to reproduce the problem locally by re-running the VOPR with that seed against that commit — because (as chapter 2 established) replay is only guaranteed relative to the code that produced it, the commit is as load-bearing as the seed itself.

FoundationDB's correctness service, Joshua, reruns a specific failing test by setting the JOSHUA_SEED environment variable to the recorded seed. In practice this comes with a documented environmental caveat beyond "same seed, same commit": simulation determinism also depends on the exact build environment — a binary compiled against libstdc++ versus libc++, or built in a different container/OS image than the one the original failure ran in, is not guaranteed to reproduce the identical execution, because subtle differences in floating-point, hashing, or memory-layout behavior can desync the replay before it ever reaches the bug.

FoundationDB's own debugging tools are the clearest existing example of "determinism-preserving observability": tr.debugTransaction() combined with debugRandom() turns on detailed tracing for one specific transaction inside a simulation run without changing the deterministic randomness stream that produced the original failure — the trace is read off the run, never fed back into it. Separately, fdbserver --print-sim-time surfaces the simulated clock (not the wall clock) when a run appears to hang, which is the only clock whose value means anything inside a discrete-event simulation.

This resolves the Heisenbug problem from chapter 1 in the specific case of DST, rather than sidestepping it. A real concurrent system's bug can vanish under a debugger because attaching one perturbs OS thread-scheduling timing. A deterministic simulator's schedule is not a function of OS timing at all — it's a function of the seeded PRNG stream (chapter 2) — so an observability call that only reads state and writes it out, without itself consuming a random draw, blocking on real I/O, or reading the real wall clock, cannot perturb the schedule, because it was never part of what the schedule depends on. The instrument only becomes a Heisenbug again if it reaches around the injected clock/RNG/scheduler the same way any other leak would (chapter 2's leak pitfall) — e.g. a logging helper that calls a real timestamp function, or accidentally draws from the same RNG the simulation uses for its own decisions and shifts every later value downstream.

Zeller and Hildebrandt's delta-debugging algorithm, ddmin, automates exactly the "binary search through execution" intuition: given a failing test case, it splits the input into halves, tests each half (and its complement) against the failure, keeps whichever still fails, and recurses — converging on a 1-minimal case where removing any single remaining element makes the failure disappear. Their original evaluation minimized a Mozilla crash from 95 recorded user actions down to 3, and 896 lines of failure-inducing HTML down to a single line, fully automatically.

Applied to a DST failure, the object being bisected should be the seed's underlying choice sequence (the stream of scheduling/fault/workload decisions the PRNG produced), not the derived event trace directly — the same "integrated shrinking" principle chapter 5 introduced for minimizing a workload generalizes directly to minimizing a debugging session: each bisection candidate is replayed through the same generator/simulator, so it is guaranteed to be a legal execution, and a run that takes thousands of events to fail typically bisects down to its minimal cause in on the order of log2(n) replays rather than a linear read of the whole trace.

Because a discrete-event simulator runs single-threaded and holds all state in one process, taking a full checkpoint at any event boundary is just a snapshot of in-memory state and the event queue — cheap enough to take often. That is what makes "time travel" through a failing run practical in a way it structurally cannot be for a general record-and-replay debugger on a real multi-threaded program: a developer can seek to any event index in an already-recorded failing run and resume forward or re-diverge from there, rather than only ever being able to single-step forward from the start.

Antithesis's causality analysis operationalizes "which earlier event actually caused this failure, versus which merely preceded it" as a search rather than a guess: starting from one observed bug timeline, it rewinds to a series of earlier moments and, from each, re-explores forward multiple times with different fuzzer decisions, tracking what fraction of those re-explorations still hit the same bug. Plotted as bug-probability over time, a sharp jump in that probability at a given moment identifies the event that causally mattered — the tool is finding the cause programmatically, rather than a developer eyeballing a long trace and guessing which of hundreds of preceding events was the one that counted.

Academic "causal slicing" / dynamic-slicing techniques for concurrent and message-passing programs generalize the same idea outside any one vendor's tooling: instead of reading an entire recorded execution, the technique reconstructs only the events that are causally connected to the failure — by data dependency, control dependency, or (for distributed/message-passing systems) causal message ordering — and discards the rest. The payoff is the same as minimization: a trace with thousands of events collapses to the handful that actually explain the failure, because most of a long trace is causally irrelevant noise relative to any one bug.

A minimized reproducer is a debugging tool, not just a triage nicety: a smaller, causally-tight failure is faster for a human to read, easier to reason about, and — critically — much less likely to get accidentally "fixed" by an unrelated later change, because there is less surrounding code for that change to coincidentally touch. This is the same discipline the workloads chapter introduced for minimizing a failing seed before shrinking it, now applied specifically to the act of debugging rather than only to producing a clean bug report.

Because a seed's reproducibility is conditional on the exact code (and, per Joshua's caveat, the exact build environment), the standard practice across DST-using teams is to treat a freshly minimized failure as raw material for a permanent artifact, not as the permanent artifact itself: convert the minimized fault schedule/workload shape into a concrete, hand-written regression scenario that is checked in and runs on every future build, rather than relying on the original seed number to keep reproducing the bug as the codebase moves on underneath it.

Real DST programs run at (at least) three distinct cadences, each doing a job the others structurally cannot. Per-PR: RisingWave runs each deterministic test with 16 different seeds in parallel and keeps a full PR's worth of simulation tests inside roughly a 20-minute budget, relying on simulated time running 4-to-5x faster than real time to fit meaningfully more coverage into that window than an equivalent real-time integration-test run could. Continuous/background: FoundationDB's Joshua service runs large "ensembles" of test runs around the clock against a coordinating cluster — enough volume that the documented expectation is every code probe (BUGGIFY site) gets hit at least once in a nightly run — and TigerBeetle's Continuous Fuzzing Orchestrator (CFO) runs a dedicated machine cluster continuously, with results published to a public dashboard (devhub) and a `fuzz` GitHub label a developer can apply to steer extra fuzzing attention at one specific PR.

Pre-release burst: TigerBeetle's fuzzing fleet runs 24/7 on roughly 1024 dedicated CPU cores with simulated time accelerated on the order of 700x, which the project describes as simulating on the order of two millennia of cluster faults-and-recoveries every single day — a concentrated, standing investment of compute specifically so that, ahead of any release, an enormous amount of adversarial history has already been explored against the current code rather than left to chance.

The three cadences are complementary, not redundant, precisely because of what each one trades away: the per-PR tier is fast and shallow by necessity (a developer is waiting on it), the continuous/nightly tier is deep but has latency (a bug it finds may already be a day old by the time anyone sees it), and the pre-release burst is the deepest of all but only runs occasionally. A program that only runs one of the three either blocks every PR on a search too shallow to find most of what DST is for, or lets bugs sit undetected in the mainline for however long the slow tier takes to notice them.

snippets.note: Illustrative -- the general shape of FoundationDB's debugTransaction()/debugRandom() guarantee: an observability call is determinism-preserving exactly when it only reads simulated state, never real time, real randomness, or a real blocking call.

Illustrative -- the ddmin binary-partition idea (Zeller & Hildebrandt) applied to a DST fault schedule; same shape as chapter 5's shrink(), reframed here as the developer's actual debugging loop rather than an automated pre-commit pass.

pitfalls: Treating "I saved the seed" as sufficient for reproducibility. Per chapter 2, replay is conditional on the exact commit too; Joshua's own documentation goes one step further and warns that even seed+commit isn't enough if the build environment differs (a libstdc++-vs-libc++ swap, a different container image) -- the full reproducibility contract is seed, code, and build environment together.

Reading a full raw event trace linearly instead of minimizing or causally slicing it first. A failing run can carry thousands of events; the vast majority are causally irrelevant to the bug, and reading them in order wastes the debugging session on noise a bisection or slicing pass would have discarded in minutes.

Adding an ordinary-looking debug print or log statement that happens to call a real timestamp function, touch real randomness, or block on real I/O. This silently desyncs the simulation's schedule -- the exact Heisenbug failure mode from chapter 1, reimported through the back door of "just add a log line" instead of through concurrency.

Manually deleting events from a fault schedule or trace ad hoc to "simplify" it, instead of bisecting systematically. An event that looks irrelevant can be a hidden causal prerequisite for a later one; removing it by hand can silently produce a trace that no longer reproduces the bug at all, or reproduces a different one.

Running DST at only one cadence. A per-PR-only strategy is structurally too shallow (the time budget can't cover the state space); a nightly-only strategy lets bugs sit undetected in mainline for a day or more; skipping a pre-release burst forgoes the deepest, most compute-intensive pass right when it matters most.

Letting a minimized failing seed be the only artifact for a found bug, rather than converting it into a checked-in, hand-written regression scenario. A routine upstream code change can silently shift where later PRNG draws land in the stream and invalidate the seed's path back to the bug -- with no separate regression test, that coverage disappears with no failure to notice.

claims.text: FoundationDB's own documentation is explicit that simulation is not able to reliably detect performance issues, such as an imperfect load-balancing algorithm, and that it is also unable to test third-party libraries or dependencies, or even first-party code not implemented in Flow (FDB's actor-based concurrency framework). As a direct consequence, FoundationDB has largely avoided taking dependencies on external systems in the first place, precisely because those dependencies would sit outside what simulation can exercise.

The same mechanism that makes discrete-event simulation fast is exactly why it is a poor tool for judging real performance: a discrete-event simulator can fast-forward its clock straight to the next scheduled event whenever nothing is happening, so a run with long stretches of low utilization completes in a tiny fraction of the wall-clock time a real system would take to reach the same state. That's what lets a simulated night explore vastly more of the state space than the equivalent real time would allow — but it also means the simulator's notion of elapsed time is not a faithful stand-in for real latency or throughput under real contention, so a clean simulated run says nothing reliable about whether the real system is fast enough.

Bugs in a critical dependent system such as a filesystem or operating system, or a misunderstanding of its contract, can produce bugs in FoundationDB that simulation alone would not catch, because the simulator models the abstraction it was given (a POSIX-like disk interface), not the exact fault behavior of a specific kernel or filesystem build underneath it.

OS and filesystem contract misunderstandings are a documented, recurring class of real-world bugs distinct from anything a simulator's fault model would think to inject: PostgreSQL's fsync() surprise showed that on Linux, an fsync() call that fails can silently mark the affected dirty pages as clean, so a later retry of fsync() reports success even though the original write was never durably persisted — a kernel behavior no application-level simulated-disk model assumed at the time. Pillai et al. (OSDI 2014) separately found hundreds of crash-vulnerabilities across widely used filesystems and applications by testing actual OS/filesystem behavior, not a simulated approximation of it.

Real hardware exposes fault classes that a container-based or purely in-process simulated environment structurally cannot: Jepsen's own tooling documentation notes that containers (LXC and Docker) can't change system clocks, so testing anything that relies on clock skew requires running nodes as separate physical machines or full VMs instead — the fault itself only exists once there is a real clock to desynchronize.

The idea that a simulated test environment diverges from the real environment it stands in for is well established outside software as the 'reality gap' or 'sim-to-real gap' in robotics and autonomous-systems testing: a simulator's fidelity is always a mismatch between the model's mathematical/physical approximations and the full complexity of real sensing, actuation, and environments, and that gap grows or shrinks with how much fidelity the simulator was built to have. The same structural idea applies to software DST — a simulated network, disk, or scheduler is a chosen abstraction, not the real thing, and its 'simulation gap' is exactly the set of real-world behaviors that abstraction was never built to reproduce.

FoundationDB's own stated practice is to run simulation alongside — not instead of — live performance testing and hardware-based failure testing, explicitly because simulation and these other techniques catch different, non-overlapping classes of problems: simulation is exhaustive over logical/correctness scenarios but is a poor tool for judging real throughput, latency under real contention, or real hardware failure behavior.

Datadog's engineering team combined three distinct techniques to validate their Courier message-queuing service, each catching a different class of problem: TLA+ formal modeling exhaustively checked correctness properties across millions of distinct reachable states (their model checker explored 5,515,710 distinct states without finding a violation of a 'no lost messages' property) but had to abstract away real implementation details (e.g., FoundationDB's optimistic concurrency control) to stay tractable; a lightweight discrete-event simulation (built with SimPy) then predicted realistic performance under node-failure scenarios, revealing an oscillating-throughput pattern from CPU load redistribution that the formal model had no way to surface since it doesn't reason about performance at all; and chaos testing against the real, running implementation then confirmed that production behavior actually matched what the simulation predicted — the one step that can catch a case where the real code doesn't do what either model assumed.

Formal methods (TLA+ and similar specification languages) sit at a different point on the same trade-off as DST: a formal spec explores the reachable state space of a deliberately abstracted model exhaustively (or near-exhaustively) and can catch a design-level correctness bug before a line of implementation code is written, but the guarantee only covers the model, not the implementation — a correct spec can still have an incorrect implementation, and specifying a system formally typically requires abstracting away details (concrete data structures, specific concurrency-control mechanisms) that DST, running real code, does not have to abstract away at all.

Adopting DST against an existing, already-shipping codebase is widely reported as materially harder than designing for it from day one: retrofitting determinism into code that was not built with clock/RNG/IO abstractions from the start is difficult, because every hidden source of nondeterminism has to be found and routed through a seed-controlled seam, and any one missed source can undermine determinism for the whole system. Tools that simulate at the hypervisor/OS boundary (Antithesis) sidestep source-level retrofitting entirely by intercepting nondeterminism beneath an unmodified guest, trading a smaller code-change footprint for a coarser, black-box fault surface — the same simulation-first-versus-hypervisor-first trade-off chapter 3 already established, now viewed specifically through an adoption-cost lens.

Reported DST speedups over real-time testing are large but tool- and workload-specific: WarpStream has reported simulating roughly 280 logical hours of its system's behavior within about 6 hours of real wall-clock time using Antithesis — illustrative of the throughput advantage simulated/accelerated time gives state-space exploration, but a number specific to that workload and infrastructure rather than a general constant.

An incremental adoption path for an existing service mirrors the same architectural seam chapter 3 already introduced for building a simulator from scratch: wrap the highest-value, highest-bug-cost subsystem behind ports/adapters first (the boundary Cockburn's hexagonal architecture describes), inject an explicit clock and RNG at that boundary, and grow the simulated surface outward module by module — the same incremental, boundary-by-boundary substitution that the 'strangler fig' pattern uses for legacy-system migration generally, applied here to simulation coverage instead of a rewrite.

pitfalls: Treating a clean DST run as proof the system is production-ready: DST's own maintainers are explicit that it cannot reliably catch performance regressions, real hardware failure behavior, or bugs in third-party/OS-level dependencies outside its simulated boundary.

Assuming a bigger or more realistic simulator closes the simulation gap for free — higher fidelity costs more implementation and maintenance effort, and some real-world behaviors (kernel fsync semantics, real filesystem crash consistency, real clock hardware) are impractical to model faithfully at all, which is exactly why they need a complementary real-environment technique instead.

Retrofitting DST onto an existing codebase without a plan: missing even one hidden source of nondeterminism (a stray real-time call, an unseeded library RNG) can silently undermine determinism for the entire system, not just the code path that used it.

Treating 'we added a formal spec' or 'we added chaos tests' as redundant with DST rather than complementary — each technique in this chapter's map catches a materially different class of bug, and dropping any one reopens exactly the gap it was covering.

claims.text: MadSim ("Magical Deterministic Simulator for distributed systems in Rust") is a real, publicly available async runtime, API-compatible with the surface of Tokio and common networking crates, whose stated design goal is borrowed directly from FoundationDB (and sled's internal simulation guide): application code written against its APIs runs unmodified against either the real Tokio runtime in production or MadSim's simulated, seeded time/network/task scheduler in tests — the same simulation-first pattern chapter 3 described, already implemented and shipping as a Rust crate rather than a from-scratch build.

MadRaft is a public, runnable teaching lab (derived from MIT 6.824's Raft and KV-store assignments) that implements a Raft-replicated key-value store on top of MadSim specifically to teach deterministic simulation testing hands-on — its own README frames its three headline features as deterministic simulation ("catch a rare bug and then reproduce it at any time you want"), discrete-event simulation ("no time wasted on sleep — the full test can be completed in a few seconds"), and fully async code.

MadRaft's failure output demonstrates the seed-as-bug-report pattern end to end: a failing test prints a line like `MADSIM_TEST_SEED=1629626496` alongside the panic, and re-running the exact same test with that environment variable set reproduces the identical failure — the seed alone, not a saved log or trace file, is what a developer pastes into a bug report or a regression test.

MadRaft exposes a `MADSIM_TEST_NUM` environment variable that reruns a single test under many different seeds in one command (its README suggests 100 for a release-mode confidence pass) — this is the swarm/seed-farm idea from chapter 5 and chapter 8's CI cadences, available as a one-line flag rather than custom tooling.

Determinism in a Rust simulation harness like MadSim is a property the harness offers, not one it can force onto arbitrary application code: MadRaft's own documentation warns that a solution can still be nondeterministic despite running on a deterministic simulator, and lists concrete leaks a capstone builder should watch for — calling `rand::thread_rng()` instead of the simulator's seeded RNG (`madsim::rand::rng`), using `futures::select!` (which is documented to have non-deterministic branch-polling order under ties) instead of `futures::select_biased!`, and iterating a `HashMap` (whose iteration order is randomized per-process by default in Rust) instead of an order-stable structure like a `BTreeMap` or a sorted `Vec`.

MadRaft ships a `MADSIM_TEST_CHECK_DETERMINISTIC=1` mode that runs the same test at least twice under the identical seed and panics immediately if the two runs diverge — an automated, always-on check for exactly the kind of silent entropy leak (chapter 2's 'eighth leak' problem) that would otherwise only surface much later as an unreproducible failure.

A Raft-replicated key-value store is a natural, well-scoped capstone target because its correctness properties are exactly the ones this book's oracle chapter already named: no committed write is ever lost, every client sees a consistent (linearizable) view of the key space, and after faults stop, the cluster eventually elects a leader and resumes serving requests — safety and liveness both, on a system small enough for one person to build and instrument in a single project.

pitfalls: Building the simulator and the reference oracle as an afterthought once the store 'basically works' — write the state-machine reference model and the CHECK-phase comparison first (chapter 6), so the very first swarm run already has something capable of catching the bug the capstone plants later.

Treating a green run after the fix as proof the bug is gone rather than re-running the exact failing seed first — the fastest confirmation a fix actually closes the gap is replaying the seed that used to fail and watching the oracle pass on the identical schedule, not a fresh random sweep.

Letting the capstone's own application code call an unseeded RNG, iterate a HashMap, or use a non-biased select — MadRaft's documented leaks are the general-purpose list; any one of them silently reintroduces exactly the kind of entropy chapter 2 spent a whole chapter teaching you to route around.

Stopping at 'found and fixed' instead of 'found, fixed, and pinned' — per chapter 2 and chapter 8, the failing seed is only guaranteed to reproduce against the exact commit it was captured on; the capstone isn't finished until the scenario is a checked-in regression test that runs on every future change, independent of whether that seed's PRNG path still lands on the bug.

Choosing a fault schedule so aggressive (every node crashing every few ticks) that almost every run fails for uninteresting reasons — an unrealistic fault combination (chapter 7) makes the oracle noisy and the one bug worth finding gets lost in a sea of expected-looking failures.
